los.text: Describe the main signs, investigations, diagnosis and principles of treatment of diarrhoea (osmotic, secretory, inflammatory, abnormal motility)
los.html:
Definition≥3 loose/watery stools per day. Acute <14 days (mostly infective); persistent 14–30 d; chronic >4 weeks.
HistoryOnset, frequency, blood/mucus, nocturnal symptoms (organic cause), travel, food contacts, antibiotics (C. difficile), weight loss, FHx of IBD or colorectal cancer.
Signs of dehydrationDry mucosa, ↓skin turgor, tachycardia, postural hypotension, oliguria, ↑CRT.
Investigations
  • Stool MC&S, ova/cysts/parasites, C. difficile toxin
  • FBC, U&E (↓K⁺, AKI), CRP
  • Faecal calprotectin (IBD vs IBS)
  • Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA)
  • TFTs
  • FIT
  • Colonoscopy if red flags.
Treatment
  • Oral rehydration (glucose-Na⁺ co-transport still works in secretory diarrhoea)
  • IV fluids if severe
  • Treat cause
  • Antibiotics only for specific organisms or systemic illness.
TypeClueExamples
OsmoticStops on fasting; ↑stool osmotic gap (>125)Lactose intolerance, laxatives (lactulose, Mg²⁺), coeliac
SecretoryPersists on fasting; large volume; low gap (<50)Cholera, ETEC, VIPoma, carcinoid, bile acid diarrhoea
InflammatoryBlood, pus, fever, ↑calprotectinIBD, Shigella, Campylobacter, C. difficile
MotilityAlternating habit, no bloodIBS, hyperthyroidism, diabetic neuropathy
Red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, age >50 with change in habit, nocturnal diarrhoea, anaemia, FHx bowel cancer → urgent investigation.

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology of diarrhoea (osmotic, secretory, inflammatory, abnormal motility)
los.html:
Osmotic
  • Poorly absorbed solutes stay in the lumen and pull water in.
  • Stool osmotic gap = 290 − 2(Na⁺ + K⁺) is high.
Secretory
  • Active Cl⁻ secretion via CFTR in crypts
  • Water follows.
  • Cholera toxin → Gs stays on → ↑cAMP → CFTR open.
  • ETEC heat-labile toxin works the same way
  • Heat-stable toxin → ↑cGMP.
Inflammatory/exudativeMucosal damage → loss of absorptive surface, exudation of blood/protein/mucus, cytokine-driven secretion.
Abnormal motilityRapid transit → too little contact time for absorption (hyperthyroidism, IBS-D, post-vagotomy). Slow transit can cause bacterial overgrowth → diarrhoea.
Often mixed: e.g. coeliac = osmotic (malabsorbed nutrients) + inflammatory.
Secretory diarrhoea continues when fasting; osmotic diarrhoea stops.

los.text: Apply the pharmacology of drugs used to treat diarrhoeal disorders and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Oral rehydration salts (ORS)Glucose + Na⁺ co-transport (SGLT1) drags water in. First line, especially in children and the elderly.
Loperamide
  • Peripheral μ-opioid agonist
  • ↓peristalsis, ↑anal tone
  • Doesn't cross BBB.
  • Avoid in bloody diarrhoea/fever (dysentery) and C. difficile (risk of toxic megacolon).
Codeine phosphateOpioid antimotility; central side effects, dependence.
Bismuth subsalicylateAntisecretory and mildly antimicrobial; black stools.
Bile acid sequestrants(colestyramine)Bile acid diarrhoea (e.g. post-ileal resection).
Antibiotics
  • Only when indicated.
  • Clarithromycin/azithromycin for severe Campylobacter
  • C. difficile: oral vancomycin first line, fidaxomicin second line
  • Stop the culprit antibiotic and PPIs.
ProbioticsWeak evidence; may reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

los.text: Describe the structure and function of the GI, and secretion and reabsorption of sodium, potassium and water in the various segments of the alimentary canal
los.html:
Wall layersMucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae) → submucosa (Meissner plexus) → muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, Auerbach/myenteric plexus between) → serosa/adventitia.
Daily fluid
  • About 9 L enters (2 L diet + 7 L secretions).
  • The small intestine absorbs about 7.5 L (mostly jejunum), the colon about 1.4 L, and about 0.1 L is lost in stool.
JejunumLeaky epithelium; Na⁺ absorbed with glucose/amino acids (SGLT1); water follows passively.
IleumNa⁺/H⁺ exchange + Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchange; bile salts and B12 absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Colon
  • Tight epithelium.
  • Electrogenic Na⁺ absorption via ENaC (↑ by aldosterone) and short-chain fatty acid-coupled uptake.
  • K⁺ is secreted, which is why diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia.
SecretionCl⁻ via CFTR in crypt cells (cAMP/Ca²⁺-driven); HCO₃⁻ from duodenum/pancreas.

los.text: Describe how nutrients are absorbed across the GI tract and the mechanisms controlling large intestine motility and defecation
sessions: BMS 2: Nutrient absorption and large intestine motility
los.html:
CarbohydratesBrush-border disaccharidases → glucose/galactose via SGLT1 (Na⁺-coupled); fructose via GLUT5; all exit basolaterally via GLUT2.
ProteinsPeptidases → amino acids (Na⁺-coupled carriers) and di/tripeptides (PepT1, H⁺-coupled).
FatsBile salt micelles → enterocyte → re-esterified → chylomicrons → lacteals/lymph.
OthersIron and calcium in duodenum; folate in jejunum; B12 + bile salts in terminal ileum.
Colon motilityHaustral (segmental) mixing; mass movements 1–3×/day, often triggered by the gastrocolic reflex after meals.
Defecation
  • Rectal distension → rectoanal inhibitory reflex (internal sphincter relaxes, involuntary, autonomic).
  • Voluntary relaxation of the external sphincter and puborectalis (pudendal nerve, S2–4), plus Valsalva.

los.text: Describe the main components of the intracellular and extracellular fluid, and how hydrostatic and oncotic pressure influence fluid movement
sessions: BMS 3: ECF, ICF and fluid balance
los.html:
• Total body water ≈ 60% of body weight in men (≈ 42 L in a 70 kg man)
    • ⅔ ICF, ⅓ ECF.
    • ECF splits ¾ interstitial, ¼ plasma.
  • ICF: K⁺ (≈150 mmol/L), Mg²⁺, phosphate, proteins. ECF: Na⁺ (≈140), Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻. Gradients are maintained by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
  • Starling forces across capillaries: net filtration = Kf[(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)].
    • Hydrostatic pressure (Pc) pushes fluid out; higher at the arteriolar end.
    • Oncotic pressure (πc) from plasma proteins (mainly albumin) pulls fluid in.
  • Net filtration at the arteriolar end and net reabsorption at the venular end. The excess (≈2–4 L/day) returns via lymphatics.
  • Water crosses cell membranes by osmosis (aquaporins), so ICF/ECF shift with ECF osmolality.

los.text: Describe the mechanisms for disordered movement of water and solutes and how this may present
los.html:
Oedema
  • Excess interstitial fluid. Mechanisms:
  • ↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure: heart failure, DVT, venous insufficiency, fluid overload, Ca²⁺-channel blockers.
  • ↓ oncotic pressure (low albumin): nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy.
  • ↑ capillary permeability: inflammation, sepsis, burns, anaphylaxis.
  • Lymphatic obstruction: lymphoedema (malignancy, node clearance, filariasis), which is non-pitting.
PresentationPitting peripheral oedema, sacral oedema in bed-bound patients, ascites, pleural effusion, pulmonary oedema (crackles, orthopnoea).
Osmotic shifts
  • Hypotonic ECF (hyponatraemia) → water enters cells → cerebral oedema (confusion, seizures).
  • Hypertonic ECF (hypernatraemia, hyperglycaemia) → cells shrink.
  • Correct chronic hyponatraemia slowly (≤10 mmol/L per 24 h) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Unilateral swelling → think local (DVT, cellulitis, lymphatic). Bilateral → think systemic (heart, liver, kidney, drugs, low albumin).

los.text: Identify the parts of the gastrointestinal tract histologically
los.html:
OesophagusNon-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium; submucosal glands; muscle is skeletal (upper third) → mixed → smooth (lower third).
Stomach
  • Simple columnar mucus-secreting surface
  • Gastric pits/glands with parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor; eosinophilic) and chief cells (pepsinogen; basophilic)
  • Rugae
  • Extra oblique muscle layer.
DuodenumVilli + Brunner's glands in submucosa (alkaline mucus).
JejunumTall, numerous villi; prominent plicae circulares; no Brunner's glands, few Peyer's patches.
IleumShorter villi, more goblet cells, Peyer's patches in mucosa/submucosa.
ColonNo villi; straight crypts packed with goblet cells; taeniae coli.
Anal canalColumnar → stratified squamous at the dentate (pectinate) line.
